$comment: The gate-declaration finding inventory: every finding harness/gate_check.py can report, the severity it is reported at, and the exact command that fixes it. The set of ids here is asserted equal to FINDINGS in harness/gate_check.py by test_every_gate_finding_the_checker_can_emit_is_declared — in BOTH directions, because a finding the inventory does not describe is a finding nobody was told about, and an inventory entry the checker cannot reach is a promise nobody keeps. The `remediate` strings are the third field of the mirror and the reason this file exists: MD13's most transferable finding about yamine's Check struct was that every message carries the exact remediation command, because a check that says only "not ok" makes the reader go and look, and the reader who does not look is why it is still broken next week.

findings.claim: the CI workflow the declaration names never invokes the gate.
findings.remediate: add a step running the declared argv; a declaration CI does not call is a claim, not a gate

findings.claim: the declaration names a CI workflow that is not in this repository.
findings.remediate: point gate.ci.workflow at the workflow that exists, or drop the ci block if there is none

findings.claim: the declaration says nothing about CI, so nothing checks that CI runs this gate.
findings.remediate: add a ci block naming the workflow and the argv it runs

findings.claim: the declared gate command names a file in this repository that is not there.
findings.remediate: point gate.command at the file that exists, or restore the file it names

findings.claim: the declared gate command starts with a bare name that is not on PATH on this machine.
findings.remediate: run `command -v <name>`; a PATH lookup depends on the machine, so this is a warning and not a failure

findings.claim: the repository declares no gate, so the gate can only be discovered by getting it wrong.
findings.remediate: write gate.yml; schemas/gate.schema.json is the format and docs/gate.md is the worked example

findings.claim: the declaration is not a YAML document core's reader accepts.
findings.remediate: run: python3 harness/bin/gate-check <repo> --explain, and read the file and line it names

findings.claim: the declared gate entrypoint is not a file in this repository.
findings.remediate: point gate.entrypoint at the file that exists, or restore the file it names

findings.claim: the declared gate entrypoint exists but cannot be run.
findings.remediate: chmod +x the file; a gate nobody can execute is documentation

findings.claim: the gate emitted its proof with a count below the floor the declaration promised.
findings.remediate: raise the count, or raise gate.proof[].minimum deliberately; a suite that shrank is a change, not a pass

findings.claim: the gate exited nonzero.
findings.remediate: read the log path this run reported; it holds the gate's own output, which this file deliberately does not print

findings.claim: a declared proof cannot be evaluated: its pattern does not compile, or it has a floor and no single capture group to read it from.
findings.remediate: fix gate.proof[].match as a Python regular expression, with exactly one capture group when `minimum` is set

findings.claim: the gate ran, exited zero, and did not emit a proof it declared — a command that exits zero is not a gate.
findings.remediate: make the gate print the line gate.proof[].match names, or delete the proof if the gate genuinely never prints it

findings.claim: an external requirement is not satisfiable as declared: its command names a file in this repository that is not there, or names no command at all.
findings.remediate: point satisfy.command at the file that exists, or at a bare command name for something on PATH

findings.claim: an external requirement is not proven on this machine, by design.
findings.remediate: satisfy it with the declared command before gating; a requirement nobody ran is not a requirement met

findings.claim: the declaration does not satisfy schemas/gate.schema.json.
findings.remediate: run: python3 harness/bin/gate-check <repo> --explain, for the constraint and the JSON path

findings.claim: the declaration names a mise task and this repository has no mise config.
findings.remediate: add a mise.toml with that task, or drop gate.miseTask if there is no mise here

findings.claim: the declaration names a mise task that is not in this repository's mise config.
findings.remediate: add the task to mise.toml, or point gate.miseTask at the task that exists

findings.claim: this repository has a mise config and the declaration names no mise task, so the fleet's spelling is unavailable.
findings.remediate: add gate.miseTask naming the task `mise run prime` resolves to

findings.claim: the mise task's `run` is a shell string this checker cannot resolve without a shell.
findings.remediate: point `run` at a single executable, or accept that only the entrypoint on disk is cross-checked

findings.claim: the mise task's `run` string does not resolve to the declared gate entrypoint.
findings.remediate: make the task's `run` name the same file gate.entrypoint names; the two are the same gate and they may not disagree

findings.claim: the gate ran past gate.timeoutSeconds and was stopped.
findings.remediate: raise gate.timeoutSeconds deliberately, or find what the gate is waiting for

notEnforced.claim: An external requirement is actually satisfied on the machine running the check.
notEnforced.why: harness/gate_check.py checks that a requirement names an argv you can paste, and that an argv whose first element is a repository-relative path resolves to a file that is there. It does NOT run the command, and it does not pretend to have: a checker that started Postgres to see whether a database was up would be a checker whose answer depends on whether Docker is running, and would be red on a laptop and green on CI. So an unverifiable requirement is `gate.requirement-unproven`, a WARNING, and it never moves the exit code. Satisfying it is the caller's job, before gating, not the checker's — and the exit code cannot pretend otherwise. This is the same hole MD12 names: the machinery can prove "41 tests ran"; only an assertion inside the test proves "41 tests hit Postgres".

notEnforced.claim: The gate's output means what it says. A proof that a suite ran is not a proof that the tests touched the dependency they claim to.
notEnforced.why: `gate.proof` is deliberately weak: it matches a line of output. A suite that prints "1430/1430 passed" against an empty database proves that 1430 tests ran and says nothing about the schema. Making the proof strong — a collect-then-run set diff, an assertion that a connection was opened — is MD12's collect-then-run machinery and it is owed in `caf`, as `caf gate`, by a different worker. This checker is a checker of DECLARATIONS, and adding tier logic to it would have been the scope this packet explicitly rules out. What this file can prove and does is stated in docs/gate.md; what it cannot is here.

notEnforced.claim: The CI workflow does what its steps say, in the order it says.
notEnforced.why: `gate.ci-disagrees` reads the workflow textually and asks one question: does any step's `run:` body mention every element of the declared `ci.invokes` argv. That catches the failure this format exists for — a declaration that names a gate CI never calls. It does not evaluate GitHub Actions: a `run:` body can branch on an event, be skipped by a path filter, or be inside a job that never runs on this branch, and none of that is visible from the text. core's own CI therefore runs gate-check with --prove as a step of its own, which is the check the text cannot do.
